"'''The Waldo Moment'''" is the third episode in the second series of the British science fiction [[anthology series|anthology]] television series ''[[Black Mirror]]''. It was written by series creator and showrunner [[Charlie Brooker]] and directed by Bryn Higgins, and first aired on [[Channel 4]] on 25 February 2013. The episode originated in an idea for ''[[Nathan Barley]]'', an earlier TV show by Brooker and [[Chris Morris (satirist)|Chris Morris]].

The episode tells the story of Jamie Salter ([[Daniel Rigby]]), an unhappy and disillusioned comedian who plays a blue animated bear called Waldo in a satirical television programme. {{anchor|monroe}}After a politician he interviewed—Liam Monroe ([[Tobias Menzies]])—enters a [[by-election]] to become [[Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)|member of parliament]], Waldo stands as a candidate. Meanwhile, Jamie and another candidate, Gwendolyn Harris ([[Chloe Pirrie]]), develop feelings for each other. Waldo's popularity continues to rise, but Jamie, whose life is torn between his career and his role, becomes increasingly discontented with the role he is playing.

The episode is in contrast to other ''Black Mirror'' episodes with its contemporary setting; it explores public distrust of politicians. Initially based in part on the politician and future British prime minister [[Boris Johnson]], the character of Waldo was widely compared to business magnate [[Donald Trump]] following his successful [[Donald Trump 2016 presidential campaign|2016 campaign]] to become President of the United States. The episode was considered by critics to be very poor in comparison to other ''Black Mirror'' episodes, with criticisms made of its reliance on tropes and its ending. The characters of Waldo and Jamie received mixed reception.

==Plot==
<!-- Per [[MOS:TVPLOT]], the plot summary of Wikipedia articles about television episodes must be no longer than 400 words. -->
On a topical comedy show, Jamie Salter ([[Daniel Rigby]]) plays Waldo—a vulgar, animated blue bear who interviews public figures under the pretense of a children's television programme. After [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative]] politician Liam Monroe ([[Tobias Menzies]]) files a complaint over his interview, a [[television pilot]] starring Waldo is commissioned. Despite this, Jamie is disillusioned and unsatisfied with his life, particularly over a recent breakup. Executive Jack Napier ([[Jason Flemyng]]) notes that Monroe is standing to become a [[Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)|member of parliament]] in the [[by-election]] for the fictional [[United Kingdom constituencies|constituency]] of Stentonford and Hersham. It is agreed that Waldo should also stand.

Appearing as Waldo via video screens on the side of a van, Jamie goads Monroe into confrontation as he campaigns. Meanwhile, Gwendolyn Harris ([[Chloe Pirrie]]) has been chosen as the [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour Party]] candidate, though the constituency is a [[safe seat]] for the Conservatives. Harris and Jamie get drunk together, Jamie expressing his displeasure at being stuck as Waldo and Harris admitting she will not win. They have sex and agree to continue their relationship. Harris' campaign manager, Roy (Michael Shaeffer), is alarmed that she talked to Jamie, telling her that she cannot see him during the campaign.

Waldo and the other candidates are invited to a student-organised [[hustings]], in which Monroe details Jamie's mostly unsuccessful television career and derides his message as meaningless. Jamie attacks both Monroe and Harris as disingenuous career politicians, using information Harris divulged during their encounter. Waldo's rant goes viral on [[YouTube]] and receives media coverage; Waldo is interviewed by political pundit Philip Crane ([[Pip Torrens]]). Jamie, whose life is torn between his career and his role, is reluctant to continue as Waldo but does so after Jack threatens to play him instead. Afterward, Jack and Jamie meet with American agent Jeff Carter ([[David Ajala]]), who talks about the advantages of a cartoon figurehead over a human in spreading political messages abroad.

Jamie attempts to apologise to Harris, but she is furious with him and runs off. The next day, Jamie [[Breaking character|breaks character]] and urges everyone not to vote for Waldo; Jack assumes his role as Waldo and frivolously rants to invite a member of the public to assault Jamie. In the hospital, Jamie sees the results of the election: Monroe won, Waldo was second, and Harris was third, though Jack, using Waldo, incites a riot. In the final scene, a homeless Jamie is ordered to move on by the police. He sees a screen displaying Waldo on every channel, in different languages. Out of frustration, Jamie throws a bottle at it, but the police tase and attack him.

==Production==

|video1 = "[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZJdJdJUhaIc Waldo Trailer]"<br />A trailer for "The Waldo Moment"
|video2 = "[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=B12tr8APqsw The Waldo Moment]"<br />A behind-the-scenes look at the episode

"The Waldo Moment" was the third episode of the second series of ''[[Black Mirror]]'', produced by Zeppotron for [[Endemol]]. It aired on [[Channel 4]] on 25 February 2013 at 10 p.m.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.radiotimes.com/news/2013-02-25/daniel-rigby-in-charlie-brookers-black-mirror-the-waldo-moment-trailer/|title=Daniel Rigby in Charlie Brooker's Black Mirror: The Waldo Moment – trailer|work=[[Radio Times]]|last=Cole|first=Tom|date=25 February 2013|access-date=21 September 2019}}</ref> On 22 January 2013, a trailer for the second series was released, featuring a dream sequence, a factory location and a large dust cloud. The advert ran on Channel 4 and in cinemas.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.digitalartsonline.co.uk/news/motion-graphics/mpc-creates-darkly-compelling-ads-for-charlie-brookers-black-mirror/|title=MPC creates darkly compelling ads for Charlie Brooker's Black Mirror|work=Digital Arts|date=29 January 2013|access-date=16 December 2017}}</ref> A trailer for "The Waldo Moment" premiered on 19 February 2013.<ref>{{cite AV media |date=19 February 2013 |title=The Waldo Moment |medium=Video |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZJdJdJUhaIc |access-date=21 September 2019 |publisher=[[Channel 4]] (via [[YouTube]])}}</ref>

===Conception and writing===
[[File:Chris Morris 2010.jpg|thumb|alt=photo|upright=0.7|[[Chris Morris (satirist)|Chris Morris]], with whom Brooker conceived the initial idea for "The Waldo Moment"]]
The episode was written by series creator [[Charlie Brooker]]. It originates from an idea by Brooker and [[Chris Morris (satirist)|Chris Morris]], conceived when the pair were writing ''[[Nathan Barley]]'' in 2005. They imagined a politician based on the British virtual band [[Gorillaz]], whose members are animated cartoon characters. When Brooker came to write the episode, he took inspiration for Waldo's character on British politician [[Boris Johnson]],<ref name="Vulture interview"/><ref name="TimeOut">{{cite web|url=https://www.timeout.com/london/tv-and-radio-guide/charlie-brooker-and-hayley-atwell-discuss-black-mirror|title=Charlie Brooker and Hayley Atwell discuss 'Black Mirror'|work=[[Time Out (magazine)|Time Out]]|last=Tate|first=Gabriel|date=31 January 2013|access-date=16 December 2017}}</ref> and [[Ali G]] was also an inspiration.<ref name="BBC">{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/entertainment-arts-37714850|title=Black Mirror: Backlash against writer inspired episode|publisher=[[BBC]]|last=Jones|first=Emma|date=21 October 2016|access-date=16 December 2017}}</ref> [[Jón Gnarr]], a stand-up comedian who became mayor of [[Reykjavík]], was another reference point, and after the episode idea was conceived.<ref name="Wired interview">{{cite magazine|url=https://www.wired.co.uk/article/charlie-brooker|title=Charlie Brooker Q&A: the drug of tech has us hooked. What's the side-effect?|last=Kelly|first=Stephen|magazine=[[Wired (magazine)|Wired]]|date=11 February 2013|access-date=16 December 2017}}</ref>

Brooker said that the episode is "asking what satire's about". Some of Jamie's dialogue is based on Brooker's own perspective from his career, such as co-presenting ''[[10 O'Clock Live]]'', a political comedy which ran from 2011 to 2013.<ref name="ibm"/> Brooker commented that the episode was rushed due to time constraints, as he was busy rewriting drafts of another series two episode, "[[White Bear (Black Mirror)|White Bear]]". He had wanted to do more research, though he did consult with his sister-in-law [[Rupa Huq]], a then-Labour politician. Brooker said in 2018 that the idea should have been executed in a longer format, such as a two-part episode, miniseries or movie. He also wanted Jamie to be in more jeopardy, and to further develop the idea of Waldo as a "lightning rod for dissatisfaction with politicians".<ref name="ibm"/> He expressed regret at rejecting the idea of having Gwendolyn and Jamie be ex-partners.<ref name="ibm">{{cite book | title=  Inside Black Mirror | date = November 2018 | first1 = Charlie | last1 = Brooker | first2 = Annabel | last2 = Jones | first3 = Jason | last3 = Arnopp | chapter = The Waldo Moment | isbn = 9781984823489 | publisher =  [[Crown Publishing Group]] | place = New York City }}</ref>

===Pre-production===
Brooker based Waldo on Ratz, a virtual floating cat head from the first series of 1990s children's show ''[[Live & Kicking]]''. As Waldo was controlled live during filming, using state-of-the-art [[Digital puppetry|live animation techniques]], several months of pre-production work was done at the design studio Painting Practice. Staff at [[Passion Pictures]] worked on animation, having recently developed the animated meerkat Aleksandr for the advertising campaign [[Compare the Meerkat]].<ref name="ibm"/>

===Filming===
Bryn Higgins directed the episode. Describing the comedy as "implicit", Higgins aimed to film the episode in the style of a "fairly slick modern thriller". The technology shown in the episode was not too far beyond what was possible at the time, as Brooker wanted the episode to veer away from science fiction. The rig used mapped the emotions and facial movements of the performer onto the Waldo character, and it is seen in the episode. As well as Rigby, four puppeteers controlled Waldo, assigned to the roles of his eyes, his mouth, his body and the rest. Brooker requested Waldo's animation to be purposefully clunky so that the viewer would believe that Jamie was controlling him live.<ref name="ibm"/>

The Waldo van was taken to [[High Wycombe]], a town in southeast England, where members of the public were involved in interacting with Waldo. Due to legal concerns, Waldo's penis was not shown in public. Following Liam Monroe's line "He's making the whole system look absurd. Which it may well be, but it built these roads", it was planned for the car to go over a pothole, but this was cut as it looked like a camera mistake.<ref name="ibm"/>

==Analysis==
"The Waldo Moment" is a [[political satire]] and [[dystopia]]; it features aspects of dark humour.<ref name="DoG Lambie">{{cite web|url=https://www.denofgeek.com/tv/black-mirror-series-2-episode-3-the-waldo-moment-spoiler-filled-review/|title=Black Mirror series 2 episode 3: The Waldo Moment spoiler-filled review|work=[[Den of Geek]]|last=Lambie|first=Ryan|date=26 February 2013|access-date=21 September 2019}}</ref><ref name="ds ranking"/><ref name="collider ranking"/> It differs from most previous episodes in its lack of science fiction elements and absence of technology as a key theme.<ref name="DoG Lambie"/><ref name="collider ranking"/><ref name="HuffPost"/> It bears similarities to the programme's first episode, "[[The National Anthem (Black Mirror)|The National Anthem]]", which also has a storyline where "the political process is subverted by the general public's insatiable appetite for stupidity and scandal", according to Sam Parker of ''[[HuffPost]]''.<ref name="HuffPost"/>

"The Waldo Moment" explores distrust and apathy towards politicians.<ref name="DoG Lambie"/> Ryan Lambie of [[Den of Geek]] summarised the episode's message in the phrase "self-absorption will be the death of politics",<ref name="DoG Lambie"/> whilst Parker felt that the episode demonstrated "a desire for a more honest form of politics".<ref name="HuffPost">{{cite news|url=https://www.huffingtonpost.co.uk/sam-parker/black-mirror-review-the-waldo-moment_b_2764672.html|title=Black Mirror: 'The Waldo Moment' (review)|work=[[HuffPost]]|last=Parker|first=Sam|date=28 April 2013|access-date=21 September 2019}}</ref> Serena Davies of ''[[The Daily Telegraph|The Telegraph]]'' commented that the episode was "a mockery of the deeply compromised ideals of modern politics", whilst reminding viewers that politicians are "all we've got".<ref name="Telegraph">{{cite web|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/culture/tvandradio/9893606/Black-Mirror-The-Waldo-Moment-Channel-4-review.html|title=Black Mirror: The Waldo Moment, Channel 4, review|work=[[The Daily Telegraph|The Telegraph]]|last=Davies|first=Serena|date=25 February 2013|access-date=21 September 2019}}</ref> Morgan Jeffery of ''[[Digital Spy]]'' analysed that the episode criticises satire and "those who persecute others without having anything meaningful to say",<ref name="DS">{{cite web|url=https://www.digitalspy.com/tv/a461004/black-mirror-series-two-the-waldo-moment-review/|title='Black Mirror' series two 'The Waldo Moment' review|work=[[Digital Spy]]|last=Jeffery|first=Morgan|date=25 February 2013|access-date=21 September 2019}}</ref> and [[Emily Yoshida]] of ''[[Grantland]]'' believed that it exposed the issues of "cheap humour" being leveraged by politicians.<ref name="Grantland">{{cite web|url=https://grantland.com/hollywood-prospectus/black-mirror-episode-6-the-waldo-moment-vote-for-stupid/|title=Black Mirror Episode 6, 'The Waldo Moment': Vote for Stupid|work=[[Grantland]]|last=Yoshida|first=Emily|date=18 December 2013|access-date=21 September 2019}}</ref>

{{multiple image|align=right|total_width=350|image1=Boris Johnson official portrait (cropped).jpg|alt1=Boris Johnson|image2=Donald Trump official portrait.jpg|alt2=Donald Trump|footer=Politicians [[Boris Johnson]] and [[Donald Trump]] were widely compared to the character of Waldo, with Brooker describing the figures as "entertainers" who "upend normality".<ref name="BBC"/>}}
Boris Johnson, a British politician who became prime minister in 2019, was an inspiration for Waldo's character. Brooker described Johnson as "quite a clown", opining that his image "inoculated him from criticism" and set him apart from other politicians, who were seen as "bland robots parroting the same platitudes".<ref name="Vulture interview">{{cite web|url=https://www.vulture.com/2016/10/black-mirror-charlie-brooker-c-v-r.html|title=''Black Mirror'' Creator Charlie Brooker on Predicting Trump, Brexit, and How the Internet Is Making Us Crazy|work=[[Vulture (magazine)|Vulture]]|last=Singal|first=Jesse|date=16 October 2016|access-date=21 September 2019}}</ref> Three years after the episode aired, in 2016, the [[Donald Trump 2016 presidential campaign|presidential campaign]] of [[Donald Trump]] began to take off. "The Waldo Moment" was seen as prescient with regards to Trump.<ref name="Vulture interview"/><ref name="DoG Morris">{{cite web|url=https://www.denofgeek.com/tv/black-mirror-the-unexpected-foresight-of-the-waldo-moment/|title=Black Mirror: the unexpected prescience of its least-loved episode|work=[[Den of Geek]]|last=Morris|first=Brogan|date=20 January 2017|access-date=21 September 2019}}</ref><ref name="THR Apple"/> Several news reports, including one by [[Chris Cillizza]], political reporter for ''[[The Washington Post]]'', compared [[Donald Trump presidential campaign, 2016#Campaign|Donald Trump's 2016 presidential campaign]] to the episode.<ref name="WP-20150908">{{cite news |last=Cillizza |first=Chris |authorlink= Chris Cillizza |title=Donald Trump's troll game of Jeb Bush: A+ |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/the-fix/wp/2015/09/08/donald-trumps-troll-game-of-jeb-bush-a/ |date=8 September 2015 |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |access-date=24 October 2015 }}</ref><ref name="DC-20150807">{{cite news |last=O'Keefe |first=Meghan |title=Why You Must Watch ''Black Mirror'': 'The Waldo Moment' This Weekend |url=http://decider.com/2015/08/07/black-mirror-the-waldo-effect-2016-presidential-race/ |date=7 August 2015 |work=Decider |access-date=24 October 2015}}</ref> Brooker also compared Trump to Waldo, describing the latter as "an anti-politics candidate who's raucous and defensive" and "offers nothing".<ref name="THR interview">{{cite web | url = https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/live-feed/black-mirror-creator-charlie-brooker-season-3-donald-trump-940324 | title = 'Black Mirror' Creator on How He (Unknowingly) Predicted the Rise of Donald Trump, Season 3 | first = Alex |last = Ritman | date = 21 October 2016 | access-date = 15 December 2017 | work = [[The Hollywood Reporter]] }}</ref><ref name="wrap ranking"/> Brooker said that Trump and Johnson were both "entertainers" who "upend normality",<ref name="BBC"/> and successfully predicted in September 2016 that Trump would win the election.<ref name="Daily Beast">{{cite news |last=Yamato |first=Jen |title='Black Mirror' Creator Predicts Trump Will Be President: 'I Find It F*cking Terrifying' |url=http://www.thedailybeast.com/articles/2016/09/13/black-mirror-creator-predicts-trump-will-be-president-i-find-it-f-cking-terrifying.html |date=13 September 2016 |work=[[The Daily Beast]] |access-date=21 September 2019 }}</ref> On the night that Trump was elected, the [[Twitter]] account for ''Black Mirror'' posted in response: "This isn't an episode. This isn't marketing. This is reality."<ref name="DoG Morris"/>

The episode has also been compared to the [[2019 Ukrainian presidential election|2019 election]] of [[Volodymyr Zelenskyy]], a satirical actor and comedian, as President of Ukraine.<ref>{{Cite web | url = https://www.bbc.com/news/stories-47980484 | title = Ukraine election: What a TV box set may tell us about the future | date = 19 April 2019 | access-date = 21 September 2019 | work = [[BBC]] }}</ref> Zelenskyy's campaign was almost exclusively restricted to the internet, with Adrian Karatnycky of ''[[Politico]]'' commenting that his campaign resembled Waldo's in that he "made no public speeches, held no rallies and gave no press conferences". Like Waldo, Zelenskyy had few clear policy positions prior to election.<ref name="Politico">{{Cite web | url = https://www.politico.com/magazine/story/2019/04/24/ukraine-president-virtual-campaign-226711/ | title = The World Just Witnessed the First Entirely Virtual Presidential Campaign | date = 24 April 2019 | access-date = 21 September 2019 | work = [[Politico]] |last=Karatnycky |first=Adrian }}</ref> The character of Waldo was also compared to "Professor Pongoo", a candidate in the [[2012 Scottish local elections]] who dressed as a penguin and received more first-preference votes than the [[Liberal Democrats (UK)|Liberal Democrats]].<ref name="Wired interview"/><ref name="ArtsDesk"/> The technology in the episode was later compared with "[[animoji]]"—avatars in the style of [[emoji]] which animate in coordination with the user's facial movements. Animoji were announced in 2017 as a new feature of the [[iPhone X]], and resembled the technology used to animate the fictional Waldo.<ref name="THR Apple">{{Cite web | url = https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/live-feed/black-mirror-predicted-new-apple-technology-1038237 | title = How 'Black Mirror' Predicted New Apple Technology | first = Jackie | last = Strause | date = 12 September 2017 | access-date = 15 December 2017 | work = [[The Hollywood Reporter]] }}</ref><ref>{{cite news | url = https://www.telegraph.co.uk/tv/2017/09/13/black-mirror-predicted-new-iphone-x-feature/ | title = Black Mirror predicted a new iPhone X feature | date = 13 September 2017 | access-date = 15 December 2017 | work = [[The Daily Telegraph]] }}</ref>

==Reception==
The episode aired on [[Channel 4]] at 10 p.m. on 25 February 2013, and was watched by 1.28 million viewers, according to 7-day data from [[BARB]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.barb.co.uk/viewing-data/weekly-top-30|title=Weekly top 30 programmes|publisher=[[Broadcasters' Audience Research Board]]|access-date=10 December 2017}}</ref> In contrast to previous episodes, it drew poor critical reviews at the time of broadcast.<ref name="DoG Morris"/> On the [[review aggregator]] website [[Rotten Tomatoes]], it holds an approval rating of 50% based on 16 reviews, with an average rating of 6.00/10. The website's critics consensus reads: "'The Waldo Moment' aims for sharp political commentary, but comes off as uninspired as the obnoxious cartoon that runs for office."<ref>{{cite web|title=Black Mirror: Season 2, Episode 3|url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/tv/black_mirror/s02/e03|website=[[Rotten Tomatoes]]|publisher=[[Fandango Media|Fandango]]|access-date=21 September 2021}}</ref> It was considered to be the weakest episode to date by Yoshida and the weakest of the series by Parker and Richard Edwards of ''[[GamesRadar+]]'',<ref name="HuffPost"/><ref name="Grantland"/><ref name="GamesRadar"/> though Luke Owen of ''Flickering Myth'' found it to be the "best and most ambitious" of the series.<ref name="Flickering Myth"/> "The Waldo Moment" garnered ratings of four out of five stars in ''[[The Arts Desk]]'',<ref name="ArtsDesk"/> 3.5 out of five stars in ''[[GamesRadar+]]'',<ref name="GamesRadar">{{cite web|url=https://www.gamesradar.com/black-mirror-2-03-the-waldo-moment-review/|title=Black Mirror 2.03 "The Waldo Moment" Review|last=Edwards|first=Richard|work=[[GamesRadar+]]|date=26 February 2013|access-date=22 September 2019}}</ref> three out of five stars in ''[[HuffPost]]'' and ''The Telegraph'',<ref name="HuffPost"/><ref name="Telegraph"/> and a C+ rating in ''[[The A.V. Club]]''.<ref name="AVClub">{{cite web|url=https://www.avclub.com/black-mirror-the-waldo-moment-1798179015|title=''Black Mirror'': "The Waldo Moment"|work=[[The A.V. Club]]|last=Sims|first=David|date=17 December 2013|access-date=21 September 2019}}</ref>

The characters of Jamie and Waldo received mixed reviews. David Sims of ''The A.V. Club'' criticised the "frustratingly vague" motivations of Jamie's character, who was "poorly sketched out".<ref name="AVClub"/> Sims further reviewed that Waldo failed to be funny or to make meaningful comments.<ref name="AVClub"/> Edwards also criticised Waldo's dialogue and called him "too two-dimensional".<ref name="GamesRadar"/> He did, however, laud Waldo's virtual appearance and interactivity as a "fantastic premise" which was "brilliantly executed".<ref name="GamesRadar"/> Lisa-Marie Ferla of ''[[The Arts Desk]]'' praised the "perfectly-pitched comedy" in Waldo's speech on the student-organised panel.<ref name="ArtsDesk">{{cite web|url=https://www.theartsdesk.com/tv/black-mirror-waldo-moment-channel-4|title=Black Mirror: The Waldo Moment, Channel 4|work=[[The Arts Desk]]|last=Ferla|first=Lisa-Marie|date=26 February 2013|access-date=22 September 2019}}</ref>

The writing was poorly received, with Parker describing it as "unfocused".<ref name="HuffPost"/> Edwards found the storyline to be predictable and filled with tropes and Parker wrote that the characterisation in the episode was "riddled with stereotypes".<ref name="HuffPost"/><ref name="GamesRadar"/> Owen criticised that conclusions to the relationship of Gwendolyn and Jamie was "merely (an) afterthought".<ref name="Flickering Myth"/> Sims criticised the American think-tank meeting as "the laziest kind of spoofery",<ref name="AVClub"/> and Edwards concurred, calling it "totally unconvincing".<ref name="GamesRadar"/> However, in praise of the writing, Yoshida, Ferla and Owen believed the episode's storyline to be plausible.<ref name="Grantland"/><ref name="ArtsDesk"/><ref name="Flickering Myth"/>

The ending was widely criticised. Lambie described it as "sudden" and "on-the-nose",<ref name="DoG Lambie"/> Sims opined that it was "ludicrous",<ref name="AVClub"/> and Jeffery and Davies called it "half-baked" and "hammy", respectively.<ref name="Telegraph"/><ref name="DS"/> Lambie believed that the episode's message was clear halfway through;<ref name="DoG Lambie"/> contrastingly, Edwards found the message to be unclear throughout.<ref name="GamesRadar"/> Owen found the episode to "cram in too much story", saying that its final quarter was paced too quickly.<ref name="Flickering Myth">{{cite web|url=https://www.flickeringmyth.com/2013/02/black-mirror-season-2-episode-3-review/|title=Black Mirror Season 2 – Episode 3 Review|work=Flickering Myth|last=Owen|first=Luke|date=28 February 2013|access-date=21 September 2019}}</ref>
